name: One-party state
scope: The one-party state as the sources define it: a governance structure in which a single party holds a legal or de facto monopoly of political power, opposition parties are outlawed or allowed only limited, controlled participation, and the party (not the electorate) is the channel of political representation (Haerpfer, International Encyclopedia of the Social Sciences; Magaloni & Kricheli 2010). It covers the Communist model (China, Cuba, North Korea, Laos, Vietnam) and the non-Communist single-party regimes, notably the African one-party states, where Nyerere's theory of 'one-party democracy' is the best-documented statement of the case for it from the inside (Masabo 2023; Nyirabu 2002). It is kept apart from the dominant-party system, where several parties compete but one wins (Encyclopedia.com 'Party Systems, Competitive'; Magaloni & Kricheli). It excludes the particular doctrines of the ruling parties (Marxism-Leninism, fascism, Juche), which are other ideologies; only what the sources say about the single-party form itself counts.

keyWorks.title: Democracy and the Party System
keyWorks.author: Julius K. Nyerere
keyWorks.quote: The foundation of Nyerere’s democratic theory is given in his 1963 essay “Democracy and the Party System.”

summary: A one-party state is a governance structure in which a single party holds a legal or de facto monopoly of political power, with opposition parties barred or only allowed controlled participation. The sources describe it as the party representing the whole society on the assumption of one unified political will, found in Communist states and in non-Communist, mostly African, regimes where Nyerere argued that one party could be democratic. It is distinguished from the dominant-party system, where competition is allowed but one party keeps winning.
